title: True & False
objectives: By the end you can write comparisons that return TRUE or FALSE, with numbers, text and cells.
about: Every comparison in Excel gives a logical value: TRUE or FALSE. You build one with a comparison operator. Use = for equal and <> for not equal. Use > and < for greater than and less than. Use >= and <= when the limit itself should count. Comparisons work on numbers, text, and cells. Text comparisons ignore upper and lower case. In maths, TRUE counts as 1 and FALSE counts as 0. Use comparisons to test targets, find late orders, or check data. They are also the building block of the IF function in the next lesson.
syntax: = (equal) · <> (not equal) · > · < · >= · <= · TRUE counts as 1, FALSE as 0 in maths

examples.scenario: A teacher checks a score against the pass mark.
examples.why: 72 is at least 60, so the comparison is TRUE.

examples.scenario: A clerk tests a region.
examples.why: Text comparisons ignore case.

examples.scenario: An accountant finds invoices that are not paid.
examples.why: <> is TRUE when the two sides differ.

examples.scenario: A manager turns a late check into a number.
examples.why: TRUE becomes 1 when it is used in maths.

watch_out: Text comparisons ignore upper and lower case, so "East" equals "east".
A number typed as text is text. Excel ranks text above every number, so convert it before comparing.
Use >= or <= when the boundary value itself should count.
recap: You can now ask yes or no questions with comparisons. Next, the IF function turns those answers into results.

steps.prompt: A teacher compares each score with the pass mark. Amina's score is in B2 and the pass mark is in D2. In C2, show TRUE if she reached the pass mark, and FALSE if not.
hints: A comparison asks a yes or no question. Which symbol means 'at least'?
Comparison symbols such as >, <, >= and <= test two values and return TRUE or FALSE. 'Reached' means equal or above, so use >=. Compare the two cells, not a typed number.
Type =B2>=D2 in C2 and press Enter. 72 is at least 60, so Excel shows TRUE.
steps.explanation: The operator >= asks whether the score is equal to or above the pass mark. The answer is TRUE or FALSE.

common_mistakes.message: A score of exactly 60 should pass. Use >= so the pass mark itself counts.
= tests for exactly the pass mark. Use >= for the pass mark or more.
That typed 60 will not follow the pass mark cell. Compare with D2.
< asks whether the score is below the pass mark, which is the opposite question.

steps.prompt: An order sheet lists each order's region in column B. In C2, show TRUE if the order is from the East region.
hints: Text in a formula needs quotation marks. Which symbol tests for equal?
The = symbol tests whether two values are equal. Put text in quotation marks, like "East". Excel ignores upper and lower case when comparing text.
Type =B2="East" in C2 and press Enter. The region is East, so Excel shows TRUE. The first = starts the formula and the second tests equality.
steps.explanation: Comparing with = tests whether the cell equals the text. Case does not matter, so east and East match.

common_mistakes.message: <> asks whether the region is not East, which is the opposite question.
That tests for West. The question is about East.
Text needs quotation marks. Without them Excel looks for a name called East.

steps.prompt: An invoice sheet shows each invoice's status in column B. In C2, show TRUE when the invoice is not yet Paid.
hints: You want TRUE for every status except Paid. Which symbol means 'not equal'?
The <> symbol means not equal to. B2<>"Paid" is TRUE for every status except Paid. NOT(B2="Paid") gives the same result.
Type =B2<>"Paid" in C2 and press Enter. The status is Open, which is not Paid, so Excel shows TRUE.
steps.explanation: <> is TRUE whenever the two sides differ, so every status except Paid gives TRUE.

common_mistakes.message: = is TRUE only for Paid, which is the opposite question. Use <> for not equal.
Text needs quotation marks. Without them Excel looks for a name called Paid.
That tests for anything except Open, so a Paid invoice would show TRUE. Test against Paid.

steps.prompt: An order took 5 days (B2) against a promise of 3 days (C2). In D2, show 1 if the order was late and 0 if it was on time, using only a comparison and no IF.
hints: TRUE counts as 1 and FALSE counts as 0 in maths. How can you turn a comparison into a number?
Multiply the comparison by 1, or put -- in front of it. Excel then converts TRUE to 1 and FALSE to 0. Put brackets around the comparison first.
Type =(B2>C2)*1 in D2 and press Enter. 5 is greater than 3, so TRUE becomes 1.
steps.explanation: Maths turns TRUE into 1 and FALSE into 0, so multiplying a comparison by 1 gives a number.

common_mistakes.message: That shows TRUE, not 1. Multiply the comparison by 1.
That is the number of days late, 2. The task wants 1 or 0.
An order that took exactly 3 days is on time. Use > so only longer orders count as late.

steps.prompt: An import saved the quantity in B2 as text. In C2, show TRUE if the quantity is 10 or more and FALSE if not. B2 holds 5.
hints: Text and numbers are compared differently. What must happen to the text before comparing?
Excel treats any text as bigger than any number, so a text 5 looks larger than 10. Convert the text to a number first, with VALUE or by putting -- in front of it.
Type =--B2>=10 in C2 and press Enter. The -- turns the text 5 into the number 5, so 5>=10 is FALSE.
steps.explanation: A text 5 is not a number, and Excel ranks text above numbers. Converting it first gives a fair comparison.

common_mistakes.message: Excel ranks text above numbers, so the text 5 counts as bigger than 10. Convert it to a number first.
The same problem: text is ranked above numbers. Convert the text first.
That is also unreliable with text. Convert B2 to a number, then compare.

title: IF Function
objectives: By the end you can use IF to return text, numbers, calculations or an empty result depending on a test.
about: IF lets a formula make a decision. You give it a test, a result for TRUE, and a result for FALSE. Excel checks the test and returns the matching result. The results can be text in quotation marks, numbers, calculations, or an empty result written as two quotation marks. Use IF for pass or fail, bonuses, fees, flags, and warnings. To use it, type =IF(, then the test, the TRUE result, and the FALSE result, separated by commas. If you leave out the FALSE result, a failed test shows FALSE.

examples.scenario: A teacher marks a test.
examples.why: The test is TRUE, so the first result is returned.

examples.scenario: A shop sets a delivery fee.
examples.why: Results can be numbers. Do not put them in quotation marks.

examples.scenario: A manager calculates a bonus.
examples.why: A result can be a calculation.

examples.scenario: A storeman flags low stock.
examples.why: Two quotation marks give a result that looks empty.

watch_out: Put text results in quotation marks. Numbers and calculations do not need them.
If you leave out the value for FALSE, IF shows FALSE when the test fails.
Choose > or >= carefully. The boundary value must go to the correct side.
recap: You can now make a formula decide between two results. Next, AND, OR and XOR let one test check several conditions.

steps.prompt: A teacher marks a test. The score is in B2 and the pass mark is 60. In C2, show Pass for 60 or more and Fail for less.
hints: IF needs a test, a result for yes and a result for no. What is the test here?
IF(test, value if true, value if false). The test is B2>=60. Put text results in quotation marks, and separate the three parts with commas.
Type =IF(B2>=60,"Pass","Fail") in C2 and press Enter. 72 is at least 60, so the result is Pass.
steps.explanation: IF checks the test and returns the first result when it is TRUE and the second when it is FALSE.

common_mistakes.message: A score of exactly 60 should pass. Use >= so the pass mark counts.
Text results need quotation marks. Without them Excel looks for names.
The results are the wrong way round. The first result is for TRUE.
With no value for FALSE, a failing score shows FALSE. Add "Fail" as the third part.

steps.prompt: A shop ships free on orders of 50 or more. Smaller orders pay a delivery fee of 4.95. The order total is in B2. In C2, show the delivery fee.
hints: The results are numbers this time. Do they need quotation marks?
Numbers do not need quotation marks. Quotation marks turn a result into text. Use 0 for free delivery and 4.95 for the fee.
Type =IF(B2>=50,0,4.95) in C2 and press Enter. 64 is at least 50, so the fee is 0.
steps.explanation: IF can return numbers as well as text. A number in quotation marks would become text.

common_mistakes.message: Quotation marks made the 0 into text. Leave numbers without quotes.
An order of exactly 50 should ship free. Use >= so 50 counts.
The results are the wrong way round. Free delivery is the TRUE result.

steps.prompt: A rep earns a 10% bonus on their sales when sales reach 5000 or more, and no bonus otherwise. Sales are in B2. In C2, work out the bonus amount.
hints: The result is a calculation, not a fixed value. Can a result part contain a formula?
Each result part can be a calculation. Use B2*10% as the TRUE result so the bonus follows the sales. Use 0 for the FALSE result.
Type =IF(B2>=5000,B2*10%,0) in C2 and press Enter. 5200 reaches 5000, so the bonus is 10% of 5200, which is 520.
steps.explanation: A result can be a calculation. When the test is TRUE, IF works out B2*10%.

common_mistakes.message: That returns the rate, 0.1, not the bonus amount. Multiply by the sales.
Multiplying by 10 gives 52000. 10% is B2*10% or B2*0.1.
That pays a bonus on every sale. Add the test for 5000 or more.
Sales of exactly 5000 should earn the bonus. Use >= so 5000 counts.

steps.prompt: Each department's actual spend is in B2 and its budget is in C2. In D2, show Over budget when spend is more than the budget, and OK otherwise.
hints: The test compares two cells. Which symbol means 'more than'?
Compare the actual spend with the budget using >. Spending exactly the budget is not over it, so > is right and >= is not.
Type =IF(B2>C2,"Over budget","OK") in D2 and press Enter. 1250 is more than 1200, so the status is Over budget.
steps.explanation: The test compares two cells, so it keeps working when either number changes.

common_mistakes.message: Spending exactly the budget is not over it. Use > instead of >=.
With no FALSE result, a department within budget shows FALSE. Add "OK".
< tests for under budget, which is the opposite question.

steps.prompt: A stock sheet should flag low stock. In C2, show Reorder when the stock in B2 is below 10, and leave the cell looking empty otherwise.
hints: The cell should look empty when stock is fine. What can an IF return that shows nothing?
Two quotation marks with nothing between them, "", give an empty text result that shows nothing. Use it as the value if false, so only low stock shows a note.
Type =IF(B2<10,"Reorder","") in C2 and press Enter. 6 is below 10, so it shows Reorder. If stock were 25, the cell would look empty.
steps.explanation: An empty text result, "", shows nothing, so the note appears only when it is needed.

common_mistakes.message: With no FALSE result, healthy stock shows the word FALSE. Use "" for an empty look.
A space is not empty text. Use two quotation marks with nothing between them.
That shows 0 for healthy stock. Use "" so the cell looks empty.
Stock of exactly 10 is not below 10. Use < for below.

title: AND, OR, XOR Functions
objectives: By the end you can combine several conditions with AND, OR, XOR and NOT, alone or inside IF.
about: AND, OR and XOR let one test check several conditions. AND returns TRUE only when every condition is TRUE. OR returns TRUE when at least one condition is TRUE. XOR returns TRUE when exactly one of two conditions is TRUE. NOT flips TRUE to FALSE and FALSE to TRUE. Each condition is a comparison, and they are separated by commas. Excel checks every condition you list. Use them for eligibility rules, ranges between two limits, and either or choices. Put one inside IF as the test to turn the answer into a result.

examples.scenario: A manager checks two bonus conditions.
examples.why: Both tests are TRUE, so AND is TRUE.

examples.scenario: A car park checks for free parking.
examples.why: One TRUE test is enough for OR.

examples.scenario: An inspector checks that exactly one approval exists.
examples.why: XOR is TRUE for exactly one TRUE test.

examples.scenario: A clerk reverses a test.
examples.why: NOT turns TRUE into FALSE.

watch_out: Write each condition as a full comparison. B2>10 and 20 is wrong, but AND(B2>10,B2<20) is right.
To test a range such as 18 to 24, use AND with two comparisons, not 18<=B2<=24.
OR is TRUE for almost any number if you test the same cell with two overlapping conditions.
recap: You can now combine conditions in one test. Next, IS functions test what a cell contains.

steps.prompt: A bonus needs two things: sales of at least 500 and the East region. The region is in B2 and sales are in C2. In D2, show TRUE only when both conditions are met.
hints: Both conditions must hold. Which function returns TRUE only when everything is TRUE?
AND(condition1, condition2, ...) returns TRUE only when every condition is TRUE. Write each test as a comparison, and separate them with commas.
Type =AND(C2>=500,B2="East") in D2 and press Enter. 650 is at least 500 and the region is East, so both tests are TRUE.
steps.explanation: AND returns TRUE only when every test inside it is TRUE.

common_mistakes.message: OR is TRUE when either test is TRUE. This bonus needs both, so use AND.
Sales of exactly 500 should qualify. Use >= so 500 counts.
Text needs quotation marks. Without them Excel looks for a name called East.

steps.prompt: Parking is free for members, or for visits under 30 minutes. Membership (Yes or No) is in B2 and minutes are in C2. In D2, show TRUE when parking is free.
hints: Either condition is enough. Which function returns TRUE when at least one test is TRUE?
OR(condition1, condition2, ...) returns TRUE when at least one condition is TRUE. It returns FALSE only when every condition is FALSE.
Type =OR(B2="Yes",C2<30) in D2 and press Enter. Sam is not a member, but 20 is under 30, so one test is TRUE.
steps.explanation: OR is TRUE as soon as any one test is TRUE.

common_mistakes.message: AND needs both tests to be TRUE. Free parking needs only one, so use OR.
A visit of exactly 30 minutes is not under 30. Use < so 30 does not count.
That tests for non-members. Test for members with B2="Yes".

steps.prompt: A lab must stay between 18 and 24 degrees, both limits included. The temperature is in B2. In C2, show TRUE when it is within range.
hints: Between means above the low limit and below the high limit. Which function joins both tests?
Test each limit separately and join them with AND. Both limits are included, so use >= for the low limit and <= for the high limit.
Type =AND(B2>=18,B2<=24) in C2 and press Enter. 21 is at least 18 and at most 24, so both tests are TRUE.
steps.explanation: A range check needs two tests joined with AND, one for each limit.

common_mistakes.message: The limits themselves are allowed. Use >= and <= so 18 and 24 count.
OR is TRUE for almost any number. A range check needs both limits, so use AND.
Excel works out 18<=B2 first and then compares TRUE with 24. Use AND with two tests.

steps.prompt: Two inspectors each answer Yes or No in B2 and C2. In D2, show TRUE when exactly one of them approved, and FALSE when both or neither did.
hints: Exactly one means one TRUE but not two. Which function is TRUE for an odd number of TRUE tests?
XOR(condition1, condition2) is TRUE when exactly one of two conditions is TRUE. It is FALSE when both are TRUE or both are FALSE.
Type =XOR(B2="Yes",C2="Yes") in D2 and press Enter. Only the first inspector approved, so the answer is TRUE.
steps.explanation: XOR is TRUE only when exactly one of the two tests is TRUE.

common_mistakes.message: OR is also TRUE when both approved. XOR is TRUE only for exactly one.
AND needs both inspectors to approve. XOR needs exactly one.
That is TRUE when the two answers match, which is the opposite question.

steps.prompt: Orders under 1000 from customers rated 4 or more are approved automatically. All others need a review. The total is in B2 and the rating is in C2. In D2, show Approve or Review.
hints: Two conditions decide the result. How can IF test both at once?
Put AND inside IF as the test. IF(AND(test1, test2), result if both, result if not). Both tests must be TRUE for Approve.
Type =IF(AND(B2<1000,C2>=4),"Approve","Review") in D2 and press Enter. 800 is under 1000 and 5 is at least 4, so the result is Approve.
steps.explanation: AND supplies a single TRUE or FALSE to IF, which then picks the result.

common_mistakes.message: OR approves an order if either test passes. Approval needs both, so use AND.
An order of exactly 1000 is not under 1000. Use < so 1000 goes to review.
A rating of exactly 4 should be approved. Use >= so 4 counts.

title: IS Functions
objectives: By the end you can test whether a cell is empty, a number, text, a logical value or an error, and react with IF.
about: IS functions test a cell and answer TRUE or FALSE. ISBLANK checks for an empty cell. ISNUMBER, ISTEXT, ISNONTEXT and ISLOGICAL check what kind of value a cell holds. ISERROR is TRUE for any error. ISNA is TRUE only for #N/A. ISERR is TRUE for every error except #N/A. None of them changes the cell they test. ISEVEN and ISODD, from lesson 23, belong to the same family. Use them to spot missing data, text hiding in number columns, and errors. Combine them with IF to show a message instead of a problem.
syntax: ISBLANK(value) · ISNUMBER(value) · ISTEXT(value) · ISNONTEXT(value) · ISLOGICAL(value) · ISERROR(value) · ISERR(value) · ISNA(value)

examples.scenario: A clerk finds missing phone numbers.
examples.why: The phone cell is empty.

examples.scenario: An analyst finds numbers saved as text.
examples.why: Text that looks like a number is still text.

examples.scenario: A manager flags errors.
examples.why: ISERROR is TRUE for any error.

examples.scenario: An analyst finds missing lookup items only.
examples.why: ISNA is TRUE only for #N/A.

watch_out: A cell that looks empty may hold a space or an empty text result. ISBLANK is FALSE for those.
Text that looks like a number is still text. ISNUMBER and ISTEXT see through the look of the cell.
ISERROR catches every error. Use ISNA when only #N/A should be treated differently.
recap: You can now test cells before you use them. Next, IFS handles many conditions in one clean formula.

steps.prompt: A customer sheet has phone numbers in column B. In C2, show TRUE when the phone number cell is empty.
hints: A function can test whether a cell is empty. Which one answers TRUE or FALSE?
ISBLANK(cell) returns TRUE when the cell is completely empty. It returns FALSE when the cell holds anything, including text or a number.
Type =ISBLANK(B2) in C2 and press Enter. B2 is empty, so the answer is TRUE.
steps.explanation: ISBLANK is TRUE only for a cell with nothing in it.

common_mistakes.message: A2 holds the customer name. Test the phone cell, B2.
ISTEXT is TRUE only when the cell holds text. An empty cell holds nothing.
ISNUMBER is TRUE only for numbers. Use ISBLANK to test for an empty cell.

steps.prompt: An import left some quantities as text. B2 holds the quantity 12 as text. In C2, show TRUE only when B2 is a real number.
hints: A number typed as text looks like a number but is not one. Which function tests for a real number?
ISNUMBER(cell) returns TRUE when the cell holds a real number, and FALSE for text, even text that looks like a number such as 12.
Type =ISNUMBER(B2) in C2 and press Enter. B2 holds the text 12, not a number, so the answer is FALSE.
steps.explanation: ISNUMBER sees through the look of the cell. Text that looks like 12 is still text.

common_mistakes.message: ISTEXT asks the opposite question and returns TRUE for the text 12.
Text is ranked above numbers, so this says TRUE for the text 12. Use ISNUMBER.
B2 is not empty. ISBLANK answers a different question.

steps.prompt: A column holds comments, but some cells contain numbers by mistake. In C2, show TRUE only when B2 holds text.
hints: You need a test that is TRUE for words and FALSE for numbers. Which function does that?
ISTEXT(cell) returns TRUE when the cell holds text, and FALSE for numbers, logical values, errors and empty cells.
Type =ISTEXT(B2) in C2 and press Enter. B2 holds the words Call back, so the answer is TRUE.
steps.explanation: ISTEXT is TRUE only for text, so a number or an empty cell gives FALSE.

common_mistakes.message: ISNONTEXT asks the opposite question. It is TRUE for numbers and empty cells.
ISNUMBER is TRUE for numbers. Use ISTEXT for words.
That is TRUE for a number as well as for text. Use ISTEXT.

steps.prompt: A results sheet sometimes shows errors. B2 may hold an error. In C2, show Check when B2 is an error of any kind, and Fine otherwise.
hints: Any error should trigger the message. Which function is TRUE for every kind of error?
ISERROR(cell) returns TRUE for any error value, such as #DIV/0! or #N/A. Put it inside IF as the test so the result becomes a message.
Type =IF(ISERROR(B2),"Check","Fine") in C2 and press Enter. B2 shows #DIV/0!, which is an error, so the result is Check.
steps.explanation: ISERROR catches every kind of error, and IF turns the answer into a readable message.

common_mistakes.message: ISNA catches only #N/A. A #DIV/0! error would be missed. Use ISERROR.
That flags good numbers and misses errors. Flag errors with ISERROR.
That tests for an empty cell. Use ISERROR to test for errors.

steps.prompt: A lookup shows #N/A when an item is missing, and other errors mean something else is wrong. In C2, show TRUE only when B2 is #N/A, not for other errors.
hints: One error type is special here. Which function is TRUE only for #N/A?
ISNA(cell) is TRUE only for #N/A. ISERROR is TRUE for every error, and ISERR is TRUE for every error except #N/A.
Type =ISNA(B2) in C2 and press Enter. B2 shows #N/A, so the answer is TRUE. A #DIV/0! error would give FALSE.
steps.explanation: ISNA separates a missing item (#N/A) from other errors, which need a different fix.

common_mistakes.message: ISERROR is TRUE for every error, including #DIV/0!. You want only #N/A.
ISERR is TRUE for every error except #N/A, so it misses this one.
B2 is not empty. ISBLANK answers a different question.

title: IFS Function
objectives: By the end you can test many conditions in one IFS formula, order the tests correctly and finish with a catch-all.
about: IFS checks several conditions in one formula, without nesting IF inside IF. You give it pairs: a test, then the result for that test. Each pair is separated by commas. Excel works through the pairs in order and returns the result of the first test that is TRUE. If no test is TRUE, IFS shows #N/A. To prevent that, end with TRUE as the last test, which always passes. Use IFS for grades, bands, tiers, and rates. Put the strictest test first, because the first match wins. IFS needs Excel 2019 or Microsoft 365.

examples.scenario: A courier bands parcels by weight.
examples.why: The first TRUE test wins.

examples.scenario: A shop sets a discount tier.
examples.why: The highest tier is tested first.

examples.scenario: A bookkeeper labels overdue invoices.
examples.why: <=0 also covers early payments.

examples.scenario: A finance clerk works out a late fee.
examples.why: Each result can be a calculation.

watch_out: Tests are checked in order and the first TRUE wins. Put the strictest test first.
With no TRUE at the end, a value that fails every test shows #N/A.
IFS needs Excel 2019 or Microsoft 365. In Excel 2016 and earlier, use nested IF instead.
recap: You can now build tiered rules in one formula. Next, SWITCH maps exact codes to results.

steps.prompt: A courier bands parcels by weight: 1 kg or less is Small, up to 5 kg is Medium, and anything heavier is Large. The weight is in B2. In C2, show the band.
hints: Three bands need three tests, checked in order. How do you end an IFS so every weight gets a result?
IFS takes pairs of a test and a result. Excel returns the result of the first TRUE test. Finish with TRUE as the last test, which catches everything left.
Type =IFS(B2<=1,"Small",B2<=5,"Medium",TRUE,"Large") in C2. 3 fails the first test and passes the second, so the band is Medium.
steps.explanation: IFS checks the tests in order and returns the result of the first one that is TRUE. The final TRUE catches everything else.

common_mistakes.message: The order is wrong. A light parcel passes B2<=5 first. Put the smallest limit first.
A heavy parcel matches no test and shows #N/A. End with TRUE and a final result.
A parcel of exactly 1 kg is Small. Use <= so 1 counts.

steps.prompt: A shop gives 10% off orders of 1000 or more, 5% off orders of 500 or more, and nothing below that. The order value is in B2. In C2, show the discount rate.
hints: The biggest discount needs the strictest test. Which test should come first?
Check the highest band first. A value of 1200 passes both B2>=500 and B2>=1000, and IFS returns the first TRUE, so the 1000 test must come before the 500 test.
Type =IFS(B2>=1000,10%,B2>=500,5%,TRUE,0) in C2 and press Enter. 700 fails the first test and passes the second, so the rate is 5%.
steps.explanation: Because IFS stops at the first TRUE, the tests must run from the most demanding to the least.

common_mistakes.message: The order is wrong. 1200 passes B2>=500 first and gets only 5%. Put the 1000 test first.
An order below 500 matches no test and shows #N/A. End with TRUE and 0.
An order of exactly 1000 earns 10%. Use >= so 1000 counts.

steps.prompt: An invoice's days overdue are in B2. Show On time for 0 or fewer days, Late for 1 to 7 days, and Very late for more than 7. Put the answer in C2.
hints: Three outcomes, three tests. Which limit goes first, and which test can end the formula?
Start with the lowest band and work upwards. A negative number of days means early, so use <=0 for On time rather than =0.
Type =IFS(B2<=0,"On time",B2<=7,"Late",TRUE,"Very late") in C2. 3 days fails the first test and passes the second, so the status is Late.
steps.explanation: Using <=0 for the first band covers early payments too, and the TRUE at the end catches everything above 7.

common_mistakes.message: An invoice paid early, with -2 days, would show Late. Use <=0 for On time.
An invoice 7 days late is Late. Use <=7 so 7 stays in that band.
Every on-time invoice passes B2<=7 first. Put the smallest limit first.

steps.prompt: A score is in B2. Show Excellent for 85 or more, Good for 70 or more, Fair for 50 or more, and Poor below 50. Put the rating in C2.
hints: Four ratings need four tests, with the highest limit first. How does the last rating get a test?
Test from the highest limit down: 85, then 70, then 50. For the last rating, use TRUE as the test, which catches every score that is left.
Type =IFS(B2>=85,"Excellent",B2>=70,"Good",B2>=50,"Fair",TRUE,"Poor") in C2. 72 passes the 70 test first, so the rating is Good.
steps.explanation: IFS returns the first match, so a score of 72 gets Good and never reaches the Fair test.

common_mistakes.message: A high score passes B2>=50 first and gets Fair. Put the highest limit first.
A score below 50 matches no test and shows #N/A. End with TRUE and Poor.
A score of exactly 85 is Excellent. Use >= so 85 counts.

steps.prompt: A late invoice's days late are in B2 and its amount is in C2. The fee is 0 for no delay, 2% of the amount up to 30 days, 5% up to 60 days, and 10% beyond. In D2, show the fee amount.
hints: Each band returns an amount, not just a rate. What must each result be multiplied by?
Each result is a percentage of the amount, so write C2*2%, C2*5% and C2*10%. Check the shortest delay first, and end with TRUE for the longest.
Type =IFS(B2<=0,0,B2<=30,C2*2%,B2<=60,C2*5%,TRUE,C2*10%) in D2. 45 days passes the 60-day test, so the fee is 5% of 400, which is 20.
steps.explanation: Each IFS result can be a calculation, so the fee is worked out from the amount.

common_mistakes.message: That returns the rate, such as 0.05, not the fee. Multiply the rate by the amount in C2.
More than 60 days matches no test and shows #N/A. End with TRUE for the 10% band.
An invoice 30 days late is in the 2% band. Use <=30 so 30 stays there.

title: SWITCH Function
objectives: By the end you can map codes to results with SWITCH, add a default, and use SWITCH(TRUE, ...) for ranges.
about: SWITCH compares one value with a list of possible matches and returns the result paired with the first match. You write the value, then match and result pairs, and finally an optional default for anything unmatched. It matches exact values only, and text matching ignores case. Without a default, an unmatched value shows #N/A. Use SWITCH for codes such as regions, day numbers, categories, and methods. It is shorter than a long IF chain. Writing the matches and results in pairs keeps the formula easy to read. SWITCH needs Excel 2019 or Microsoft 365.

examples.scenario: A clerk turns a code into a region.
examples.why: The code matches the second pair.

examples.scenario: A scheduler turns a day number into a name.
examples.why: Numbers need no quotation marks.

examples.scenario: An accountant sets a tax rate with a default.
examples.why: The default catches every other category.

examples.scenario: A teacher bands scores by switching on TRUE.
examples.why: The first test that is TRUE wins.

watch_out: SWITCH matches exact values and cannot test ranges directly. Use SWITCH(TRUE, ...) or IFS for ranges.
Write the default last, with no match beside it. Without it, an unmatched value shows #N/A.
SWITCH needs Excel 2019 or Microsoft 365. In older versions, use nested IF or CHOOSE.
recap: You can now map codes to results cleanly. Next, IF combinations bring IF, AND, OR and more together.

steps.prompt: Orders carry a one-letter region code in B2: E, W, N or S. In C2, show the full name: East, West, North or South, or Unknown for any other code.
hints: One cell is matched against several exact codes. Which function pairs a value with its result?
SWITCH(value, match1, result1, match2, result2, ..., default) compares the value with each match in turn. The last argument, with no match beside it, is the default for anything unmatched.
Type =SWITCH(B2,"E","East","W","West","N","North","S","South","Unknown") in C2. The code W matches, so the region is West.
steps.explanation: SWITCH compares the code with each match and returns the paired result. The default catches unknown codes.

common_mistakes.message: With no default, an unknown code shows #N/A. Add "Unknown" as the last argument.
W and N are paired with the wrong regions. Check each pair.
IF handles only one code. SWITCH can match all four.

steps.prompt: A rota stores the day as a number: 1 for Mon up to 7 for Sun. The number is in B2. In C2, show the day name, or Invalid for any other number.
hints: The codes are numbers this time. Do the matches need quotation marks?
Numbers in the match positions are written without quotation marks. Text results use quotation marks. Finish with a default for numbers outside 1 to 7.
Type =SWITCH(B2,1,"Mon",2,"Tue",3,"Wed",4,"Thu",5,"Fri",6,"Sat",7,"Sun","Invalid") in C2. The number 3 matches, so the day is Wed.
steps.explanation: SWITCH compares the number with each match. Number matches are written without quotation marks.

common_mistakes.message: A number outside 1 to 7 shows #N/A. Add "Invalid" as the default.
Quotation marks made the matches text, so the number 3 matches nothing. Write numbers without quotes.
Wed and Thu are swapped. Check each pair.

steps.prompt: Tax depends on the category in B2: Food is 0%, Books is 5%, and every other category is 20%. In C2, show the tax rate.
hints: Two categories are named, and everything else shares one rate. Where does that shared rate go?
Name the special categories as match and result pairs. The shared rate for all other categories goes last, as the default, with no match beside it.
Type =SWITCH(B2,"Food",0,"Books",5%,20%) in C2 and press Enter. Books matches the second pair, so the rate is 5%.
steps.explanation: A default works as an 'everything else' rule, so only the special categories need their own pairs.

common_mistakes.message: A category such as Toys matches nothing and shows #N/A. Add 20% as the default.
Quotation marks turned the rates into text. Leave numbers without quotes.
The default is 0, which gives other categories no tax. It should be 20%.

steps.prompt: An order has a shipping method code in B2 (1 Standard 4.95, 2 Express 9.95, 3 Next day 14.95) and goods worth the amount in C2. In D2, show the total including shipping. Any other code means no shipping.
hints: The shipping cost depends on the code. How can SWITCH sit inside a sum?
SWITCH returns a number, so it can be added to another cell. Use the default 0 for codes that mean no shipping, so the total is just the goods.
Type =C2+SWITCH(B2,1,4.95,2,9.95,3,14.95,0) in D2. Code 2 matches 9.95, and adding the 40 of goods gives 49.95.
steps.explanation: SWITCH can return a number that is added to other cells, so one formula builds the total.

common_mistakes.message: That shows only the shipping. Add the goods in C2.
A code outside 1 to 3 shows #N/A. Add 0 as the default.
That multiplies the goods by the shipping. Add them.

steps.prompt: A score is in B2. Use SWITCH to show A for 90 or more, B for 75 or more, C for 60 or more, and Fail below 60. SWITCH normally matches exact values, so think about what to switch on.
hints: SWITCH matches exact values, not ranges. Which value could you switch on to test conditions instead?
Give SWITCH the value TRUE, then pair each test with its result. SWITCH finds the first test that equals TRUE, so list the highest band first and end with a default.
Type =SWITCH(TRUE,B2>=90,"A",B2>=75,"B",B2>=60,"C","Fail") in C2. 82 passes the 75 test first, so the grade is B.
steps.explanation: SWITCH(TRUE, ...) matches the first test that is TRUE, which lets SWITCH handle ranges.

common_mistakes.message: That works, but this step asks for SWITCH. Switch on TRUE.
The matches are text, not tests, so nothing matches and you always get Fail. Switch on TRUE.
A score below 60 shows #N/A. Add "Fail" as the default.

title: IF Combinations
objectives: By the end you can nest IF, and combine IF with AND, OR, SUM and other functions to build real decisions.
about: Real decisions rarely fit a single simple IF. You can nest one IF inside another to handle three or more outcomes. You can put AND or OR inside IF to test several conditions at once. You can put SUM, COUNT or other functions inside the test, or inside the results. IF only works out the result it needs. So you can use it to avoid an error such as dividing by zero. Build the formula in layers. Write the plain-English rule first, then the tests, then the results, and check each boundary value.
syntax: IF(test1, result1, IF(test2, result2, result3)) · IF(AND(...), ...) · IF(OR(...), ...) · IF(SUM(...)>x, ...)

examples.scenario: A courier prices parcels in three bands.
examples.why: Each IF handles one decision.

examples.scenario: A shop gives a member discount with a spend condition.
examples.why: AND supplies the test.

examples.scenario: A help desk escalates tickets.
examples.why: OR is TRUE when either test is TRUE.

examples.scenario: An analyst avoids dividing by zero.
examples.why: The division is skipped when the units are zero.

watch_out: Check the smallest or strictest limit first in a nested IF, and check every boundary value.
Count your brackets. Each IF needs its own closing bracket, and nested IFs close at the end.
For more than three outcomes, IFS is easier to read than a long nest of IF.
recap: You can now build real decision formulas. Next, Track 05 turns to lookups: finding values in tables with VLOOKUP, XLOOKUP and INDEX/MATCH.

steps.prompt: A courier charges 3.50 for parcels up to 1 kg, 6.00 up to 5 kg, and 9.50 above that. The weight is in B2. In C2, show the price using nested IF.
hints: Three prices need two decisions. How can an IF sit inside another IF?
Put a second IF in the FALSE part of the first. IF(test1, result1, IF(test2, result2, result3)). Check the smallest limit first.
Type =IF(B2<=1,3.5,IF(B2<=5,6,9.5)) in C2 and press Enter. 2.5 fails the first test and passes the second, so the price is 6.
steps.explanation: A nested IF puts the next decision inside the FALSE part, so each test only runs when the earlier ones failed.

common_mistakes.message: The order is wrong. A light parcel passes B2<=5 first. Put the smallest limit first.
A heavy parcel shows FALSE. Add 9.5 as the last result.
A parcel of exactly 1 kg costs 3.50. Use <= so 1 stays in the first band.

steps.prompt: Members who spend 100 or more get 10% off, and everyone else gets 0. Membership (Yes or No) is in B2 and spend is in C2. In D2, show the discount.
hints: Two conditions must both be true. Which function goes inside IF as the test?
Use AND as the test: IF(AND(test1, test2), result if both, result if not). Both the membership and the spend must pass.
Type =IF(AND(B2="Yes",C2>=100),10%,0) in D2 and press Enter. Sam is a member and spent 120, so the discount is 10%.
steps.explanation: AND gives IF a single TRUE or FALSE, so the discount applies only when both tests pass.

common_mistakes.message: OR gives the discount if either test passes. It needs both, so use AND.
Spending exactly 100 should qualify. Use >= so 100 counts.
Quotation marks made the 10% text. Leave numbers without quotes.

steps.prompt: A support ticket is escalated if its priority is High or if it has waited more than 48 hours. Priority is in B2 and hours waiting are in C2. In D2, show Escalate or Normal.
hints: Either condition is enough to escalate. Which function belongs inside the IF?
Use OR as the test: IF(OR(test1, test2), result if either, result if neither). One passing test is enough.
Type =IF(OR(B2="High",C2>48),"Escalate","Normal") in D2 and press Enter. The priority is Low, but 60 is over 48, so the action is Escalate.
steps.explanation: OR is TRUE when either test passes, so IF escalates the ticket.

common_mistakes.message: AND escalates only when both tests pass. One is enough, so use OR.
A ticket that has waited exactly 48 hours is not over 48. Use > so 48 stays Normal.
A normal ticket shows FALSE. Add "Normal" as the last result.

steps.prompt: Four expenses are in B2:B5 and the budget is in D2. In F2, show Budget exceeded when the total is more than the budget, and Within budget otherwise.
hints: The test compares a total with a budget. Which function gives the total inside the test?
Put SUM inside the test: IF(SUM(range)>budget, ...). Spending exactly the budget is not over it, so use > rather than >=.
Type =IF(SUM(B2:B5)>D2,"Budget exceeded","Within budget") in F2. The total is 480, which is more than 450, so the result is Budget exceeded.
steps.explanation: SUM works inside the test, so the status updates whenever an expense changes.

common_mistakes.message: Spending exactly the budget is not exceeding it. Use > instead of >=.
That compares only the first expense with the budget. Compare the total, SUM(B2:B5).
Within budget shows FALSE. Add "Within budget" as the last result.

steps.prompt: A shop sheet shows units sold in B2 and revenue in C2. In D2, show the average price per unit, but show No units when nothing was sold.
hints: Dividing by zero causes an error. How can IF stop that division from happening?
Test for zero first. If the units are zero, return a message instead of dividing. IF only works out the result it needs, so the division is skipped.
Type =IF(B2=0,"No units",C2/B2) in D2 and press Enter. 8 units are not zero, so Excel divides 200 by 8 and shows 25.
steps.explanation: IF evaluates only the branch it needs, so the division never runs when the units are zero.

common_mistakes.message: With 0 units this shows #DIV/0!. Test for zero first.
That shows 0 instead of a message. The task wants No units.
That divides the wrong way round. The price per unit is revenue divided by units.

title: Track 04 Checkpoint: Decisions with IF
about: Three problems, one per level. Passing a level unlocks the next. Easy has hints on, Medium offers a hint only after a wrong attempt, and Hard has no hints.

steps.prompt: A chain labels each store's sales. The sales figure is in B2. In C2, show High when sales are over 100, and Low otherwise.
hints: IF needs a test, a result for yes and a result for no. What is the test?
IF(test, value if true, value if false). The test is B2>100. Put the text results in quotation marks and separate the three parts with commas.
Type =IF(B2>100,"High","Low") in C2 and press Enter. 120 is over 100, so the result is High.
steps.explanation: IF checks B2>100 and returns High when it is TRUE and Low when it is FALSE.

common_mistakes.message: Sales of exactly 100 are not over 100. Use > instead of >=.
Text results need quotation marks.
The results are the wrong way round. The first result is for TRUE.

steps.prompt: A bonus is paid when sales reach 500 or more in the East region. The region is in A2 and sales are in B2. In C2, show Bonus when both conditions are met, and None otherwise.
hints: Two conditions must both be true. Which function goes inside IF as the test?
Use AND as the test: IF(AND(test1, test2), result if both, result if not). Both the sales and the region must pass.
Type =IF(AND(B2>=500,A2="East"),"Bonus","None") in C2. 650 is at least 500 and the region is East, so the result is Bonus.
steps.explanation: AND supplies one TRUE or FALSE to IF, so the bonus appears only when both tests pass.

common_mistakes.message: OR pays a bonus if either test passes. It needs both, so use AND.
Sales of exactly 500 qualify. Use >= so 500 counts.
Without a FALSE result, a non-qualifying row shows FALSE. Add "None".

steps.prompt: A score is in B2. In C2, show the grade: A for 90 or more, B for 75 or more, C for 60 or more, and Fail otherwise.
steps.explanation: IFS returns the result of the first TRUE test, so 82 stops at the 75 test and gets B. The final TRUE catches every score below 60.

common_mistakes.message: A high score passes B2>=60 first and gets C. Put the highest limit first.
A score below 60 matches no test and shows #N/A. End with TRUE and Fail.
A score of exactly 90 is an A. Use >= so 90 counts.
